panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Low-power (4×) H&E of a shave biopsy from the right arm/forearm showing spongiotic-acanthotic epidermis with focal parakeratosis and a mixed lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular infiltrate; the in-text explicitly states these coexisting spongiotic and lichenoid features are recognised histological patterns of Grover disease rather than arguments against it. B: High-power (40×) H&E showing a focal acantholytic cleft (arrow) with dyskeratotic keratinocytes (arrowheads) at a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate; the in-text identifies recurrent focal acantholysis as the key finding supporting the diagnosis of Grover disease.

(A) Spongiotic-acanthotic epidermis with focal parakeratosis and a mixed lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular inflammatory infiltrate (original magnification 4×). (B) Focus of acantholysis (arrow) at the margin of a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate; dyskeratotic keratinocytes are indicated by arrowheads (original magnification 40×).
in_text_mentions: luent parakeratosis, a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with a lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular distribution, small foci of acantholysis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, associated with a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate (Figure 3). Although acantholysis was focal, its recurrence in specimens obtained during a separate disease episode, in the same clinical setting as the initial biopsy, was regarded as the key finding supporting the diagnosis; the coexisting spongiotic and lichenoid features are recognised histological patterns of GD rather than arguments against it (Section 3.3).

panels.attribution_text: Maghiar et al. Chronic-Recurrent, Limb-Predominant Grover Disease in a Young Adult: A Clinicopathological Diagnostic Challenge. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

in_text_mentions: haemorrhagic crusts, were distributed predominantly over the proximal upper limbs and thighs, with only discrete truncal involvement and post-inflammatory macules on the posterior trunk (Figure 1A,B). Vesicles, bullae and pustules were absent. Dermoscopy showed a nonspecific inflammatory pattern of focal pink-red erythema, fine superficial scale and superficial haemorrhagic crusts (Figure 2). No burrows and no delta-wing jet signs were identified at any of the examined sites, and there was no involvement of the interdigital web spaces or the genital skin, findings that argued against scabies.

The caption and article text describe focal hypergranulosis and suprabasal cleft containing acantholytic and dyskeratotic keratinocytes, which are characteristic histological findings for transient acantholytic dermatosis (GD), consistent with Grover's disease.

in_text_mentions: attern. Focal hypergranulosis and suprabasal clefts containing acantholytic and dyskeratotic keratinocytes were observed in the epidermis. A loose perivascular lymphoid infiltrate, which included a few eosinophils and neutrophils, was found in the superficial dermis (Figures 2 and 3). Direct immunofluorescence was negative. During hospitalization, skin lesions began to improve. The patient was discharged to the outpatient-clinic to continue follow up. Skin lesions disappeared in two months. Clinicopathologic features were consistent with the diagnosis of transient acantholytic dermatosis (GD).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E of the patient's back lesion showing the acantholytic pattern the caption attributes to all three panels; article diagnosis is Grover's disease. B: Intermediate-magnification H&E with acantholysis plus the captioned dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, part of the Grover's disease biopsy workup. C: High-power H&E showing the hallmark Darier-like dyskeratosis with corps ronds (yellow arrows) amid acantholytic keratinocytes, explicitly captioned and consistent with Grover's disease.
panels.attribution_text: Mihelcic et al. A Grover-Like Skin Rash: A Potential Indicator of Underlying Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) Infection.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.60173. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at three different magnifications, 100x (A), 200x (B), and 400x (C). All three images depict acantholysis. Image B additionally demonstrates dermal lymphocytic infiltration. Image C demonstrates dyskeratosis with the presence of corps ronds (yellow arrows) with eosinophilic cytoplasm and central pyknotic nuclei, amidst separated keratinocytes.
in_text_mentions: Bacterial and viral swabs were taken from his skin lesions were unremarkable. There was no evidence of Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1), Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Skin biopsies were taken from lesions on the back, with histopathological analysis revealing suprabasal acantholysis, dyskeratosis, corps ronds, and lymphocytic infiltration in the upper layers of the dermis, with no evidence of vasculitis (Figure 2). Direct immunofluorescence was unremarkable. This was consistent with a diagnosis of Grover’s disease.

plate_findings.evidence: Eroded erythematous to violaceous papules distributed across the back
widespread eroded erythematous papules visible over the patient's back

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of widespread eroded erythematous/violaceous papules on the back, matching the truncal papular eruption of Grover disease; the article describes it as a Grover-like rash in the context of SARS-CoV-2, so typicality is atypical. B: Close-up clinical photo of discrete crusted/eroded erythematous papules on the trunk, consistent with Grover-like papular eruption; article links it to SARS-CoV-2, hence atypical. C: Clinical photograph showing papular eruption extending over chest and abdomen with spared surrounding skin, typical truncal distribution of Grover disease; context is a Grover-like rash associated with COVID-19, so atypical.
panels.attribution_text: Mihelcic et al. A Grover-Like Skin Rash: A Potential Indicator of Underlying Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) Infection.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.60173. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A and B: Eroded erythematous to violaceous papules distributed across the back. C: Continuation of lesions over the chest and abdomen. The surrounding skin is clear.
in_text_mentions: ine-day history of an intensely pruritic rash on his back and chest, and no other associated symptoms. His past medical history was significant only for hypertension, for which he took perindopril, and he had no known drug allergies and took no over-the-counter medications or supplements. On examination, the patient was afebrile and normotensive but notably hypoxic on room air with an oxygen saturation of 90% and tachycardic with a heart rate of 120 beats per minute. Dermatological examination revealed widespread eroded erythematous papules visible over the patient’s back and chest (Figure 1).
